lead: Metal cutting creates a chip by shear. Two forces are easy to measure on a dynamometer: cutting force Fc along the cutting speed and thrust force Ft normal to it. Merchant's circle resolves their resultant R into friction F and normal N on the rake face, and into shear Fs and normal Fn on the shear plane. This tells you how much energy goes into friction and how much into shear, so you can choose rake angle, cutting fluid and feed. It is used in turning, drilling and milling force estimates.
prereq: You need: chip thickness ratio and shear angle from 5.1.

sections.h3: Force resolution on the Merchant circle

blocks.text: In orthogonal cutting the cutting edge is straight and the chip flows at right angles to it. A dynamometer measures two forces. The cutting force F<sub>c</sub> (N) acts along the cutting speed. The thrust force F<sub>t</sub> (N) acts normal to it, pushing the tool away from the work. Their resultant R = √(F<sub>c</sub>² + F<sub>t</sub>²) is the diameter of the Merchant circle.

On the rake face, R resolves into friction F (N) along the face and normal N (N) across it. The rake angle α is the angle between the rake face and the normal to the cut surface. The friction angle β is the angle between R and N, so μ = tan β = F/N. On the shear plane, R resolves into shear force F<sub>s</sub> (N) along the plane and normal force F<sub>n</sub> (N) across it. The shear plane makes shear angle φ with the cutting speed. The same R closes both resolutions, which is why one circle gives friction and shear together.
F = F<sub>c</sub> sin α + F<sub>t</sub> cos α
blocks.where: F is friction force on the rake face (N); F<sub>c</sub> cutting force (N); F<sub>t</sub> thrust force (N); α rake angle.

blocks.text: N = F<sub>c</sub> cos α − F<sub>t</sub> sin α
blocks.where: N is normal force on the rake face (N); other symbols as above.

blocks.text: Shear area A<sub>s</sub> = b t<sub>1</sub>/sin φ, where b is width of cut (mm) and t<sub>1</sub> is uncut chip thickness (mm). Shear stress on the plane is τ = F<sub>s</sub>/A<sub>s</sub> (N/mm² = MPa). Cutting power is P = F<sub>c</sub> v, where v is cutting speed in m/s and P is in W. Specific cutting energy is u = F<sub>c</sub>/(b t<sub>1</sub>) = P/MRR, where MRR = b t<sub>1</sub> v is material removal rate. u is in N/mm², numerically equal to J/cm³.
F<sub>s</sub> = F<sub>c</sub> cos φ − F<sub>t</sub> sin φ,   F<sub>n</sub> = F<sub>c</sub> sin φ + F<sub>t</sub> cos φ
blocks.where: F<sub>s</sub> shear force along shear plane (N); F<sub>n</sub> normal force across shear plane (N); φ shear angle.

blocks.text: A<sub>s</sub> = b t<sub>1</sub> / sin φ,   τ = F<sub>s</sub>/A<sub>s</sub>,   P = F<sub>c</sub> v
blocks.where: A<sub>s</sub> shear area (mm²); b width of cut (mm); t<sub>1</sub> uncut chip thickness (mm); τ shear stress (MPa); P power (W); v cutting speed (m/s).

blocks.text: Merchant's relation is 2φ + β − α = 90°. It comes from assuming the shear angle adjusts so that cutting energy is minimum. Use it as an estimate. It fails when friction is abnormal, when a built-up edge forms, or when ploughing is large.

Procedure: set b, t<sub>1</sub> and v, and measure F<sub>c</sub> and F<sub>t</sub> with a dynamometer. Compute F and N, then μ and β. Use Merchant's relation to estimate φ. Compute F<sub>s</sub>, A<sub>s</sub>, τ, P and u. Compare τ with the shear strength of the work material. A high μ means more friction on the rake face; change rake angle or cutting fluid. A high τ means the shear plane is carrying more stress; reduce feed or change speed.
Keep units consistent: Fc and Ft in N, b and t1 in mm, v in m/s for W. Merchant's relation is an approximation, not a law. Tool geometry is covered in 5.3, fluids in 5.4, and wear in 5.5.

examples.question: An orthogonal cutting test gives cutting force Fc = 1200 N, thrust force Ft = 600 N, rake angle α = 10°, uncut chip thickness t1 = 0.25 mm, width of cut b = 2.5 mm and cutting speed v = 120 m/min. Find friction force F, normal force N, friction coefficient μ, friction angle β, shear angle φ by Merchant's relation, shear stress τ on the shear plane, cutting power P and specific cutting energy u.
examples.check:
import math
Fc = 1200.0
Ft = 600.0
alpha_deg = 10.0
alpha = math.radians(alpha_deg)
t1 = 0.25
b = 2.5
v = 120.0/60.0
F = Fc*math.sin(alpha) + Ft*math.cos(alpha)
N = Fc*math.cos(alpha) - Ft*math.sin(alpha)
mu = F/N
beta_deg = math.degrees(math.atan(mu))
phi_deg = (90.0 + alpha_deg - beta_deg)/2.0
phi = math.radians(phi_deg)
Fs = Fc*math.cos(phi) - Ft*math.sin(phi)
As = b*t1/math.sin(phi)
tau = Fs/As
P_kW = Fc*v/1000.0
u = Fc/(b*t1)
print(round(F))
print(round(N))
print(round(mu, 3))
print(round(beta_deg, 1))
print(round(phi_deg, 1))
print(round(tau))
print(round(P_kW, 1))
print(round(u))

traps: Merchant's relation is a minimum-energy approximation; do not use it when friction is abnormal or a built-up edge is present.
Fs = Fc cos φ − Ft sin φ, not Fc sin φ + Ft cos φ; the sine and cosine swap between Fs and Fn.
μ = F/N, not Fc/Ft; β = tan⁻¹ μ, and α, β, φ must use the same degree or radian convention.
For power in watts, convert v from m/min to m/s; keep Fc and Ft in the same force unit before resolving.
As = b t1/sin φ; sin φ is in the denominator, and b and t1 must both be in mm.

quiz.q: Define friction angle β and write μ in terms of β.
quiz.a: β is the angle between resultant R and normal N on the rake face; μ = tan β = F/N.

quiz.q: Why does one resultant R give both rake-face and shear-plane forces?
quiz.a: R is the same vector from measured Fc and Ft. Its components depend on the plane chosen: resolving along the rake face gives F and N; resolving along the shear plane gives Fs and Fn.

quiz.q: Fc = 900 N, Ft = 300 N and α = 8°. Find F and N.
If α = 6° and β = 32°, find φ by Merchant's relation.
Why can Merchant's relation fail when a built-up edge forms?
quiz.a: A built-up edge changes the effective rake angle and friction, adds ploughing and makes forces unsteady. The minimum-energy single shear plane assumption no longer holds, so the predicted φ is unreliable.

quiz.q: What does specific cutting energy mean and what are its units?
quiz.a: It is the energy needed to remove unit volume of material: u = Fc/(b t1). Units are N/mm², equal to J/cm³.

quiz.q: A test shows μ falls but τ rises when cutting speed is increased. Give one possible reason.
quiz.a: Rake-face friction may fall due to heating or fluid action, while strain rate and a smaller shear area raise shear stress. Check for built-up edge, tool wear and temperature; Merchant's relation may not hold.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite-element machining models replace the single shear plane with a shear zone and predict stress and temperature. Industry uses dynamometer tests and specific cutting energy tables to set feeds and detect wear. Search next for Merchant circle, shear plane model, specific cutting energy and Johnson-Cook machining.
